# UX & Behavioral Design

This file is the index. The cards themselves live in `resources/`, one
file per category. Use the tables below to decide which file to open, then
read that file. Do not load every resource unless the change spans several
categories.

Rules that hold across every card:

- Prefer the smallest change that removes the failure state.
- Check the code in front of you; do not restyle unrelated code.
- A checklist item that asks for a human-subject experiment cannot be
  satisfied by reading code. Say so rather than claiming it was done.
- When two cards disagree, first check whether one describes a situation
  the other assumes. If it does, that constraint applies first and the other
  card's advice is scoped to what survives it - do not average the two into
  a compromise neither card endorses. If neither constrains the other, follow
  the more specific prescription.
- Where a fix can either remove a failure state or rearrange around it,
  removing it outranks rearranging: a layout that avoids the violation
  beats one that mitigates it.
- Name the pairs you had to weigh in the review, and which card you
  followed. A silent choice reads as an oversight; a stated one can be
  checked. The settled pairs are listed under Known tensions.

## Known tensions

Two cards can prescribe incompatible fixes. Each row below is settled: the ruling names the card that wins, and the records have been rewritten to follow it. Read the ruling before choosing between the cards.

- **DEC-01 vs MPA-01 — fixing a 12-item flat navigation.** DEC-01 wins as the constraint: the bar is five to seven destinations before MPA-01's ordering applies. MPA-01's original remedy assumed a 12-item bar, which is the situation DEC-01 removes.
- **HMM-01 (within the card) — the Cmd/Ctrl+K search shortcut.** HMM-01's never-hijack check wins over its own Cmd/Ctrl+K example: a browser command cannot be reliably taken by the page, so the remedy uses /, which the page receives before the browser's quick-find default.

## Heuristic & Mental Models (11 cards)

Read `resources/heuristic-mental-models.md` for the checks, fixes and sources.

| ID | Card | Apply when |
|---|---|---|
| HMM-01 | Jakob's Law | Users hesitate, hunt for navigation, or misuse controls because the layout diverges from conventions they know from other products. |
| HMM-02 | Mental Model Theory | Users invent their own account of how a feature works, then blame the interface when that account predicts the wrong result. |
| HMM-03 | Conceptual Integrity | Two screens in one product use different labels, layouts, or gestures for the same job, so each has to be learned from scratch. |
| HMM-04 | Aesthetic-Usability Effect | A restyle changes only color, type, and spacing; testers still rate the product easier to use and stop noticing its flaws. |
| HMM-05 | Principle of Least Astonishment (POLA) | A familiar control does something unexpected: Save clears the form, a filter reloads the page. |
| HMM-06 | Postel's Law (Robustness Principle) | Valid input is rejected over formatting, or downstream services each get a different shape. |
| HMM-07 | Occam's Razor (Principle of Parsimony) | Options and edge-case branches pile up until nobody can describe the main path. |
| HMM-08 | Conway's Law | Two teams own half a flow each, and the product asks users to cross a seam no user would draw. |
| HMM-09 | Gulf of Execution and Gulf of Evaluation | A button gives no sign it worked, so people click again and create duplicate orders. |
| HMM-10 | Affordance Theory | A control that works looks exactly like the text around it, so nobody tries it. |
| HMM-11 | Feedback Principle (Cybernetic Loop) | A long upload shows nothing until it finishes, so people reload and start it again. |

## Gestalt & Visual Perception (11 cards)

Read `resources/gestalt-visual-perception.md` for the checks, fixes and sources.

| ID | Card | Apply when |
|---|---|---|
| GES-01 | Law of Proximity | Form labels look attached to the wrong input, or unrelated actions read as one group because spacing is uniform. |
| GES-02 | Law of Similarity | Two different kinds of control share a style, or one kind is drawn three different ways. |
| GES-03 | Law of Common Region | A dashboard has no borders, so metrics read as one undifferentiated field. |
| GES-04 | Law of Prägnanz (Law of Simplicity / Good Figure) | A layout can be parsed two ways, and the harder reading is the one users settle on. |
| GES-05 | Law of Closure | A carousel stops exactly at the screen edge, so nothing signals more content. |
| GES-06 | Law of Figure/Ground | A dialog opens with no dimmed backdrop, so its text bleeds into the page behind it. |
| GES-07 | Law of Continuity (Good Continuation) | Numbers in a table centre-align, so the decimal points stagger down the column. |
| GES-08 | Law of Uniform Connectedness | Wizard steps float unconnected, so the order has to be inferred from the numbers. |
| GES-09 | Law of Common Fate | A sidebar collapses while its labels reflow at a different speed, so the panel tears. |
| GES-10 | Law of Focal Point | Every plan in a pricing table has a solid red Buy button, so none stands out. |
| GES-11 | Law of Past Experience | A green button deletes an account, or a back arrow sits on the right of the row. |

## Decision-Making & Cognitive Load (11 cards)

Read `resources/decision-making-cognitive-load.md` for the checks, fixes and sources.

| ID | Card | Apply when |
|---|---|---|
| DEC-01 | Hick's Law | Users stall or scan repeatedly when a menu or settings page presents many flat, unranked options. |
| DEC-02 | Miller's Law | Users lose track of values across long unbroken strings, forms, or dashboards with many competing figures. |
| DEC-03 | Tesler's Law | People are asked to supply details the product could derive, such as time zones, currency formats, or bank codes. |
| DEC-04 | Choice Overload | A pricing page or settings screen shows many similar options and people stall, default, or leave without choosing. |
| DEC-05 | Cognitive Load Theory | People re-read instructions, hunt for guidance, or make avoidable errors in a dense single-page form. |
| DEC-06 | Working Memory Capacity Model | A multi-step flow asks people to remember a value from an earlier step while entering data on a later one. |
| DEC-07 | Cognitive Friction | Users click a search icon, wait for the overlay, then click the field again before they can type. |
| DEC-08 | Framing Effect | Two screens state one outcome, but one stresses what is gained and the other what is lost, and choices diverge. |
| DEC-09 | Simon's Bounded Rationality and Satisficing | People page through all forty search results because nothing marks which listing is good enough to take. |
| DEC-10 | Cognitive Absorption | A notification, promotional banner, or modal interrupts a writing or coding session that was running smoothly. |
| DEC-11 | Decision Fatigue | A flow reaches its twelfth configuration question, and the last three answers were left at the default. |

## Time, Motion & Ergonomics (10 cards)

Read `resources/time-motion-ergonomics.md` for the checks, fixes and sources.

| ID | Card | Apply when |
|---|---|---|
| TME-01 | Fitts's Law | Users miss small controls or take long pointer trips for frequent actions, especially on touch screens. |
| TME-02 | Accot-Zhai Steering Law | A cursor entering a nested fly-out drifts a few pixels sideways and the menu collapses. |
| TME-03 | Doherty Threshold | A click blocks the interface for most of a second, and the person clicks again or looks away. |
| TME-04 | Perceived Performance Heuristics | An export runs for twelve seconds behind a blank screen, and people refresh because they think it froze. |
| TME-05 | Power Law of Practice | A workflow someone uses every day takes as long in month six as it did in week one. |
| TME-06 | Keystroke-Level Model | A task feels slow although no single step is slow; the time goes into small transitions. |
| TME-07 | Weber-Fechner JND Law | Two controls differ by the same amount, but one change is obvious and the other is invisible. |
| TME-08 | Gilbreth Motion Economy | A control used every few seconds sits at the far edge of the screen. |
| TME-09 | Crossman's Velocity Law (Welford's Variant) | Small icons with tight spacing are missed while larger, padded targets are hit first time. |
| TME-10 | Visual Saccadic Latency Law | A form's labels sit far from their fields, so the eye must travel for every answer. |

## Memory, Perception & Attention (11 cards)

Read `resources/memory-perception-attention.md` for the checks, fixes and sources.

| ID | Card | Apply when |
|---|---|---|
| MPA-01 | Serial Position Effect | Critical navigation or actions sit mid-list and are overlooked while first and last items dominate attention. |
| MPA-02 | Von Restorff Effect (Isolation Effect) | One row, button, or price is remembered while identical neighbors blur together. |
| MPA-03 | Zeigarnik Effect | People return days later and remember exactly where they stopped. |
| MPA-04 | Peak-End Rule | A smooth session is rated harshly because its last screen failed. |
| MPA-05 | Anchoring Bias | A suggested price, quantity, or budget shifts what people choose. |
| MPA-06 | Selective Attention and Attentional Bottleneck | Two simultaneous requests compete, and the second is missed entirely. |
| MPA-07 | Confirmation Bias | A dashboard shows only the runs that support the current plan. |
| MPA-08 | Sunk Cost Fallacy | A team keeps funding a feature because of what it has already cost. |
| MPA-09 | Loss Aversion | A change is refused for what it might lose, not weighed by what it gains. |
| MPA-10 | Goal-Gradient Effect | People start slowly on a long task and speed up near its end. |
| MPA-11 | Status Quo Bias | A setting nobody changed is treated as the one people chose. |

Every card cites one primary paper; the citation travels with the card.
